In April 1815 Mount Tambora, on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, produced the most powerful eruption in recorded history. Tens of thousands of people died, most of them not from the blast itself but from the famine and disease that followed the destruction of crops. The eruption also injected sulphur into the stratosphere, where tiny droplets reflected part of the incoming sunlight.

The effects reached far away, after a delay. In 1816, the 'year without a summer', frosts struck New England in June and persistent rain ruined harvests across much of Europe, where grain prices soared and food riots broke out. Historians caution against blaming every hardship on the volcano: Europe was still recovering from the Napoleonic Wars, and weak solar activity may have added to the cold. Climate scientists nonetheless treat Tambora as a natural experiment showing how one eruption can cool the Northern Hemisphere for a year or more.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The eruption alone explains Europe's cold weather and food riots of 1816.
Counting blast deaths alone would miss most of the eruption's victims.
Most of the victims on Sumbawa were killed directly by the blast.
Climate scientists generally recommend cooling the planet with particles.

The Hanseatic League, a network of merchant towns led by Lübeck, dominated trade in the Baltic and North Seas from the thirteenth to the fifteenth century. Unlike a state, it had no permanent army, no common treasury and no fixed list of members, and its assembly, the Diet, met irregularly and could not compel towns to attend. Its power rested instead on trading privileges in foreign offices such as those in London and Bergen; when a ruler threatened them, the towns could respond with a collective embargo.

From the late fifteenth century the League declined, as territorial states grew stronger, Dutch and English merchants competed for Baltic trade and Atlantic routes shifted commerce westwards. The last Diet met in 1669, although Lübeck, Hamburg and Bremen still called themselves Hanseatic cities long afterwards.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: By 1669 Hamburg and Bremen had stopped calling themselves Hanseatic cities.
Towns had an embargo option, but their Diet did not compel attendance.
The League could fund its wars from a common treasury paid into by all its towns.
The League's decline was caused entirely by the new Atlantic trade routes.

The Rosetta Stone was found in 1799 by French soldiers near the town of Rashid, or Rosetta, in the Nile Delta. It carries a decree of 196 BC written three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic, the everyday Egyptian script, and in ancient Greek. After the French surrender in Egypt it passed to the British, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

Because scholars could read the Greek, the stone offered a key to the other scripts, but not at once. Thomas Young showed in the 1810s that some hieroglyphs stood for sounds, notably in royal names, and in 1822 Jean-François Champollion demonstrated that the script combined sound signs with signs for whole words, helped by his knowledge of Coptic. The stone's upper portion is missing, so the hieroglyphic text is the least complete of the three; copies of the decree found elsewhere have helped to fill the gaps.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Champollion deciphered the hieroglyphs within months of the stone's discovery.
Thomas Young was probably the first to read the stone's Demotic text.
The full decree cannot come solely from the surviving hieroglyphic text.
France has formally asked the British Museum to return the stone.

For much of the twentieth century, bilingualism was thought to harm children's development, and some educators advised immigrant parents to speak only the majority language at home. Later studies reversed that view. By the early 2000s, experiments suggested that bilinguals also outperform monolinguals on tasks requiring 'executive control', such as ignoring irrelevant information, supposedly because managing two languages trains the brain.

That claim has proved hard to replicate. Several large studies found no consistent advantage once income, education and immigration background were taken into account, and a 2015 analysis reported that studies finding an advantage were more likely to be published than those that did not. Defenders reply that effects may appear only in particular groups. What is not disputed is that speaking two languages brings practical and cultural benefits and does not damage children's development.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Published studies risk overstating the executive-control advantage.
Large studies have confirmed a clear executive-control advantage.
Immigrant parents often still speak only the majority language at home.
The 2015 analysis found that most published studies used flawed methods.

Esperanto was published in 1887 by Ludwik Zamenhof, an eye doctor in Białystok, where Polish, Russian, Yiddish and German speakers lived side by side, often in mistrust. He believed a neutral second language, belonging to no nation, could ease such tensions, and he did not intend it to replace national languages. Its vocabulary draws mainly on Romance and Germanic roots, its spelling is phonetic and its grammar has sixteen rules without exceptions. Supporters claim it can be learned faster than national languages, although the research behind such claims is limited.

The language attracted an international movement and survived persecution under both Nazi Germany and Stalin's Soviet Union, which regarded its speakers with suspicion. Estimates of speakers today range from tens of thousands to two million, and perhaps a thousand people have grown up speaking it at home.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Not all Esperanto speakers have grown up speaking the language at home.
Esperanto is used mainly by people who already speak Romance languages.
Research has generally confirmed that Esperanto is learned faster.
Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union imprisoned all Esperanto speakers.

The European Union Solidarity Fund was created in 2002, after severe floods in central Europe. It helps Member States and accession countries cope with major natural disasters and, since 2020, also with major public health emergencies. It does not compensate individuals or businesses: it reimburses part of the public cost of emergency operations, such as restoring essential infrastructure, providing temporary accommodation and cleaning up, and insured damage is not eligible.

To count as 'major', direct damage must exceed three billion euros at 2011 prices or 0.6 per cent of the country's gross national income, whichever is lower. A government must apply within twelve weeks; the Commission then assesses the request and the Parliament and Council must approve the amount, so aid has often arrived months after the event. Advance payments were introduced to shorten the delay, but critics say the Fund still suits reconstruction better than immediate relief.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Since 2020 the Fund has covered health emergencies instead of natural disasters.
Most applications to the Fund have probably come from accession countries.
At EUR 200 billion GNI, direct damage must exceed EUR 1.2 billion to qualify.
Advance payments ensure that aid now arrives immediately after a disaster.

Early lighthouses relied on open fires or lamps backed by metal mirrors, which wasted much of the light they produced. In 1822 the French physicist Augustin Fresnel designed a new kind of lens made of concentric rings of glass prisms. Because each ring bent the light towards a single beam, the lens could be far thinner and lighter than a solid lens of the same power, and it sent a much larger share of the light out to sea. The first was installed at the Cordouan lighthouse in 1823, and the design soon spread around the world.

To help sailors identify them, lighthouses were given distinctive patterns of flashes, produced by rotating the lens or screening the light. Most lighthouses are now automated, and satellite navigation has reduced reliance on them, but they still serve as a backup when electronic systems fail.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Lighthouse lenses of equal power need not have equal weight.
Satellite navigation has made lighthouses unnecessary for sailors.
Fresnel lenses were probably first used to replace open fires at Cordouan.
Every lighthouse can be identified by the colour of its light alone.

Researchers distinguish loneliness from social isolation. Isolation is an objective condition, measured by how few contacts a person has, whereas loneliness is the painful feeling that one's relationships are fewer or less satisfying than one would like. The two often occur together, but not always: some people with many contacts feel lonely, while some who live largely alone do not.

Studies have linked persistent loneliness to a higher risk of heart disease, stroke and depression, although it is harder to establish how far loneliness causes these conditions and how far illness leads people to withdraw. Contrary to a common assumption, surveys in several countries find that young adults report loneliness at least as often as older people. Some governments now treat the issue as a public policy matter: the United Kingdom appointed a minister with responsibility for loneliness in 2018, and Japan followed in 2021.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A survey limited to few contacts would not include all lonely people.
Loneliness has been proven to be the direct cause of heart disease.
Older people usually report more loneliness than young adults do.
Japan appointed a minister for loneliness before the United Kingdom did.

The Bayeux Tapestry, which tells the story of the Norman conquest of England in 1066, is not strictly a tapestry. Tapestries are woven, whereas this work is an embroidery: coloured wool stitched onto strips of linen. It is about 70 metres long and only half a metre high, and it shows scenes from the events leading up to the Battle of Hastings and from the battle itself, with short Latin captions.

Most historians think it was commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William the Conqueror's half-brother, and made in England in the decade after the conquest, probably by English embroiderers. Its final section is missing, so no one knows exactly how the story originally ended. Because it presents events largely from the Norman point of view, historians use it alongside written chronicles, comparing its version with other accounts rather than treating it as a neutral record.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: An embroidery made in England need not present an English view of the conquest.
Historians treat the work as a neutral record of the conquest.
It is known for certain that Bishop Odo designed every scene himself.
The missing final section probably showed William's coronation.

In the 1860s vineyards in southern France began to die for no obvious reason. The cause turned out to be phylloxera, a tiny insect native to North America that feeds on the roots of grapevines. It had probably arrived on American vines imported for experiments, and over the next decades it spread across most of Europe's wine regions, destroying a large share of the vineyards.

American vines had evolved alongside the insect and could tolerate it, while European vines could not. After many remedies failed, including flooding vineyards and injecting chemicals into the soil, growers adopted grafting: European varieties were joined onto resistant American roots, so that the grapes remained European while the roots resisted attack. Most European vineyards are grafted today. A few areas escaped, notably those with very sandy soils, in which the insect does not thrive, and some ungrafted vines survive there.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Grafting changed only the roots of European vines, not the grapes they bore.
Flooding vineyards proved the most effective defence against phylloxera.
American vines lacked resistance to the pest that European vines had learned to tolerate.
Ungrafted vineyards survived mainly because their owners had banned American imports.

Weather forecasts are produced by computer models that start from the current state of the atmosphere and calculate how it will evolve. Because the atmosphere is chaotic, tiny errors in the starting data grow over time, a property the meteorologist Edward Lorenz described in the 1960s. Forecasters therefore run the same model many times, each run starting from slightly different initial conditions. The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, founded in 1975, runs around fifty such variations twice a day.

If most runs agree, forecasters can be confident; if they diverge widely, the forecast is uncertain. The spread also allows probabilities to be issued, such as a 70 per cent chance of rain, meaning that rain falls in about seven out of ten comparable situations. For day-to-day weather, useful predictions rarely extend beyond about two weeks, however powerful the computers become.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The Centre was founded in 1975 to test Edward Lorenz's theory of chaos.
Ensemble forecasts are generally more accurate for rain than for heat.
Agreement among the runs proves that a forecast will turn out correct.
Dry outcomes remain possible under a forecast giving rain a 70 per cent chance.
